. . . . . . . 203  Introduction A few days before Christmas several years ago, I received an email from Amy Bauer, curator of Harvard University's Sackler Museum, asking me if I could take a look at a Coptic book. At the time, I was a doctoral student working on a dissertation about Christians in papyrus documents from the ancient Egyptian city of Oxy rhynchus, and about to teach a graduate course in Coptic in the spring semester. Assuming that this Coptic book was a 19th century printed text, I replied that I would take a look at it and inquired what kind of book it was. Bauer responded: "A sixth-century manuscript".1 The very next day, I went over to the Sackler Museum, outfitted with a notebook, digital camera, a tripod, and a good deal of curiosity. When Bauer brought the object out of the magazine and unwrapped for me a stack of tiny pages enveloped in brown leather covers, I was immediately struck by its size – the codex was only as large as my palm. I deciphered the words on the first page: The Gospel of the Lots of Mary, the Mother of the Lord Jesus Christ, and wondered: What kind of gospel is this? What is the text about? Who owned and used this codex? And why is it so small? Here I tell the story of that Coptic book – rather, that Coptic booklet. Over the past century or so, manuscript finds have greatly enlarged the library of ancient Christian texts and have added multiple long lost gospels to the inventory. From the Gospels of Mary and Thomas to the recently published Gospel of Judas, these newly discovered writings have deeply enriched our understanding of early Christianity. It is interesting to open here another new gospel, one that turns out to be very different in content and contribution. In my research, I quickly discovered that our new gospel was not a story about Jesus, but a previously unknown text of Christian oracular answers that would be received in a divinatory session. Despite its designation as gospel, this book has no narrative or plot, nor does it contain sayings of Jesus. As a matter of fact, Jesus appears only sporadically. Rather, this book contains a series of oracles. These were not intended to be read in progression or even in order, but individually, after retrieving them through a divinatory procedure ascribed to lot. With the two facing pages of the opened book featuring one oracle, the book is laid out to display only one oracle at a time. People who faced difficult decisions or needed insight into the future would consult a diviner, who performed a ritual to locate an oracle in the codex and then interpreted the divinatory text. In Egypt and the wider Mediterranean world, this practice – sortilege – was both common and controversial. 1 The manuscript was displayed at the exhibition "Byzantine Women and their World", see my description in the catalogue, Luijendijk, "Miniature Codex".  Introduction 2 Sortilege While sortilege remains a relatively understudied or isolated topic in scholarship on religion of antiquity, this does not mean that it was a fringe phenomenon in ancient society.2 On the contrary, lot divination was widely practiced in antiquity, just as it is in many present cultures. Its prevalence in the ancient world is attested by biblical traditions. Although not all biblical authors approve of divination, both the Hebrew scriptures and the New Testament abound with instances where casting lots determines someone's fate. The sentiment expressed in Proverbs 16:33 conveys the concept of many lot decisions: "The lot is cast into the lap, but the decision is the Lord's alone." The divine will determines how the dice fall.3 This is, indeed, what happened to Jonah. In the book of Jonah, the sailors, about to suffer shipwreck in a terrible storm, cast lots in order to find out who had imperiled their voyage. The lot (as the reader already expects) reveals Jonah as the culprit, who had rebelled against God's specific command to preach to Nineveh. When his shipmates reluctantly throw him overboard, the storm subsides.4 Likewise, the authors of writings in the New Testament interpret the outcome of lot divination as a divine decision. In a matter as weighty as deciding Judas's replacement and thus Jesus' twelfth disciple, the remaining eleven apostles turn to sortilege. First, the disciples pray to the Lord – an important aspect of divination, which is also prescribed in later books with lot oracles. Then, as the text reports rather matter-of-factly: "They cast lots for them, and the lot fell on Matthias; and he was added to the eleven apostles" (Acts 1:20b–26). For many people today, the word "oracle" evokes the mysterious Pythia at Delphi, delivering war strategies to kings in opaque hexameters.6 Or perhaps for others, the term calls to mind the story of Alexander the Great, who undertook an arduous journey through the Egyptian desert to inquire at the Siwa oracle whether he was indeed the Son of God. Yet the practice of seeking oracles to obtain divinely-inspired answers was not exclusively the purview of the elite.7 Enslaved people consulted lot oracles about gaining freedom, pregnant women asked about giving birth, merchants wanted to know about success in business, travelers inquired about their voyage home, and emperors sought insight about the outcomes of battles. From impressive, inscribed monuments erected on public places in Asia Minor to small strips of papyrus folded into tiny sealed packages from an Egyptian martyr shrine, as well as to our new text, epigraphic and manuscript evidence show that sortilege was ubiquitous in the ancient Mediterranean world. Where could one consult an oracle in antiquity? The possibilities extend from grand sites like Delphi to a diviner with a book visiting the inquirer at home. Some people traveled far to visit the oracles of Delphi, Didyma, or Claros – sites that, as we know from inscriptions, welcomed visitors from all over the region.8 Rich people could send slaves to submit questions in their stead. But there were also opportunities for people to consult the divine without having to travel to an oracular site. Book oracles, called sortes (from the Latin sors = lot, indicating that one would obtain the answers by casting lots), allowed for consultation on the spot; the oracle could even come to the petitioner! Pieter van der Horst refers to sortes as "instant oracles",9 and Fritz Graf describes them as "oracles that preceded the event, where a preexistent answer was waiting for the question to come."10 Our codex is one such form of a mobile and ready-made tool for divination. tim debemus sub hoc exemplo sortibus credere, uel illud de Actibus Apostolorum huic testimonio copulare ubi sorte in apostolatum Matthias eligitur, cum priuilegia singulorum non possint legem facere communem). Introduction 4 The Sortes Family Our codex belongs to a large Mediterranean family of lot books and adds a new, previously unpublished, member to the sortes clan. The family consists of inscriptions, papyri, and parchment manuscripts, written in Greek, Latin, Hebrew, Syriac, Proven çal, and Coptic. In the chapters that follow, the textual relatives introduced here will situate our codex, helping us to trace the transmission of texts, formulate ideas about its use and divinatory method, and imagine an archaeological provenance. The sortes family shares several notable characteristics that allow scholars to study them as a subgenre of oracles. For one, sortes provide a way of "prognostication, or rather problem-solving, by means of the drawing of lots (sortilegium) or the casting of dice (astragalomancy), or other randomizing practices".11 Additionally, sortes directly address a person in the second person singular. Moreover, they present the answers not in poetic hexameters as oracles do, but in prose.12 Furthermore, sortes share a binary worldview with stark contrasts between good and bad events. Theirs is a world populated with adversaries and enemies, the lives of the inquirers shadowed by the threat of danger, illness, and death. Yet sortes also have their rosy side, promising happiness, a good life, abundant harvest, and prosperity. In spite of their shared characteristics, the sortes family also displays considerable diversity. Lot books differ in their method of consultation: some present clients with preformulated questions, while others provide answers to questions clients formulate themselves. In the first of these systems, the lot book contains a series of questions with short, matching answers. Have you ever wondered: "Am I to become successful?", "Will the one who is sick survive?", "Am I to escape from slander?", "Will I have an inheritance from someone?", "Will I be a teacher?", or "Have I been poisoned?"13 People who pondered such general problems could consult a lot system written in Greek called the Sortes Astrampsychi.14 This collection consisted of 92 questions and 103 answers.15 The inquiry, "Am I to become successful", could, for instance, yield the response: "You'll soon succeed for the better."16 Similarly, a person with a pressing problem about poison could receive the sage advice: "You've indeed been poisoned. Treat yourself."17 As is clear from the many copies preserved in the papyrological record, the Sortes Astrampsychi were hugely popular in Late Antiquity. They also enjoyed a long afterlife in different guises. The Sortes Family 5 600 called the Sortes Sangallenses is a Latin adaptation of the Sortes Astrampsychi (or similar lot text).18 Ticket oracles are a related divinatory system yielding specific answers. Here a client submits two almost identical, sealed tickets to a shrine: one with a query phrased positively, the other negatively. The priests hand back the ticket with the correct formulation as the divine answer. We have such tickets in Demotic, Coptic and Greek.19 In rare instances, both tickets have been preserved. A Greek example, submitted to the shrine of Saint Philoxenus in Oxyrhynchus in the sixth century, reads: O my Lord God Almighty and St.Philoxenus my patron, I beseech you by the great name of the Lord God, if it is your will and you are helping me to take the banking-business, I beseech you to bid me learn this, and speak. Its negatively-formulated twin reads: O my Lord God Almighty and St.Philoxenus my patron, I beseech you by the great name of the Lord God, if it is not your will that I speak either about the bank or about the weighing-office, to bid me learn this, in order that I may not speak.20 We will probably never know if the inquirer became a banker. But when he received back one of the tickets, he at least knew what to do. Our text belongs to the second type of lot system, where a client could pose any question and would receive a general answer, or, as satirist Lucian of Samosata put it more bluntly, an "obscure and ambiguous" answer.21 This vagueness was not the mistake of careless or ignorant composers, but was deliberate. The general and deliberately ambiguous wording of the sortes, like those in a newspaper horoscope or fortune cookie today, made them adaptable to any situation. But they also thereby exacerbated the hermeneutical vulnerability that Lucian exploits in his satire. Some of the divinatory books spring from sacred texts, such as the Greek Sortes Homericae and the Latin Sortes Virgiliae, consisting of abstracts and selected sentences from Homer and Virgil respectively.22 In Jewish, and later in Christian, circles the system was also applied to the Bible, hence the Sortes Biblicae (in Greek). This category also includes the so-called hermeneiai-manuscripts, in which short divinatory phrases preceded by the Greek word hermeneia (explanation) are penned in the margins of biblical books, most often in the Gospel of John. These exist in Greek and/or Coptic.23 Another branch of these sortes are the so-called dice-oracles. These are Greek texts, incised on large monuments and prominently displayed on the market places of cities and towns in southwestern Anatolia.24 In his study of these inscriptions, Fritz Graf showed how their placement in the public square reveals their broader function in ancient society, as these texts gave divinely-inspired advice in such matters as commerce, travel, family life, and health. Sortes and Social History 7 The most important other Coptic sortes manuscript for our booklet is its text's closest relative: an early seventh-century manuscript consisting of two palimpsest fragments from a parchment codex, found at the church of St.Colluthus in Antinoë, published by Lucia Papini in 1998.27 On the broken bifolium, only four answers remain of what was presumably a larger codex. Two of those answers are almost verbatim parallel with our codex's text (Oracles 12 and 31); the other two share sentences with our text, but in a different order. I explore this text further throughout the book. Sortes and Social History With their focus on solving everyday problems, lot books provide rich material for social historians. Polymnia Athanasiadi has remarked: Oracles were the psychiatrists of the ancient world and much more. When in distress, the individual had recourse to Apollo ... and usually went away with renewed confidence in the future. Throughout antiquity ... consultation on private matters remained a normal oracular function.28 Through these texts we enter a world both radically different from ours and yet also strikingly similar. Lot texts give us glimpses into everyday anxieties. A sense of real physical vulnerability about health, travel, love, and professional success is still very recognizable, even if mediated by texts. In order to appreciate these texts as artifacts of the ancient past, we must understand the role and function of sortes and other divinatory texts in antiquity as tools for religious consultation about large and small concerns. In the past, some scholars looked down on sortilege. For instance, Otto Stegmüller missed the point when he disparagingly states about a papyrus with hermeneia marginalia that "as regards their content, these oracles are obviously worthless".29 But those who engaged in divination took it seriously, even if others marginalized it and we moderns may be uneasy with it. While some ancient authors such as Cicero and Lucian of Samosata pointed to the potential for corruption and manipulation, we should presuppose the religious and thus practical significance of divination in the everyday lives of people.30 Insights of ethnographers such as David Zeitlyn have helped to grasp this more fully. However, such cases (which occur both in Europe and elsewhere) are aberrant. They point to the usual perceived purpose of divination: to find answers to questions. Generally, divination is used as a means of resolving problems.31 Many currently working on the topic recognize full well that these practices were an important means of decision-making in antiquity.32 Thus divination is also intensely related to power and authority, group formation, and group identity. That divination was ubiquitous and taken seriously by its ancient practitioners is clear from the ways in which it was contested by secular laws and church canons that prohibit these divinatory practices in no uncertain terms, deeming them inappropriate and dangerous.33 Government officials and emperors issued decrees against divination. For instance, in 199 CE, the Egyptian prefect sent out a circular that was to be posted in public, stipulating that all who were found to engage in divination or magic would be put to death.34 Similarly, the historian Ammianus Marcellinus reports the forced closing of the Bes ticket oracle in Abydos, Fayum, at the orders of emperor Constantius in the year 359.35 Church leaders also condemned Christian divination, naming it among a series of crimes that Christians should not commit and forbidding it repeatedly at church councils. Although earlier we observed instances where lot divination was practiced in biblical writings, church leaders could also fall back on biblical prohibitions of such practices. One law prescribed: divinatione I.1, trans. Falconer 222–3) defines divination – he refers here to the Greek word μαντική – as "the foresight and knowledge of future matters" (praesensionem et scientiam rerum futurarum). In Book II, Cicero (ibid., II.9, 378–9) disproves his brothers positive stance on divination with an emphasis on science, stating: "Now you must admit that divination is not applicable in any case where knowledge is gained through the senses" (Ad nullam igitur earum rerum, quae sensu accipiuntur, divination adhibetur). See also Denyer, "The case against divination". Lucian (Alexander the False Prophet 8, trans. The Gospel of the Lots of Mary 9 When you come into the land that the Lord your God is giving you, you must not learn to imitate the abhorrent practices of those nations. No one shall be found among you who makes a son or daughter pass through fire, or who practices divination, or is a soothsayer, or an augur, or one who casts spells, or one who consults ghosts or spirits, or who seeks oracles from the dead. ... Although these nations that you are about to dispossess do give heed to soothsayers and diviners, as for you, the Lord your God does not permit you to do so (Deut. 18:9–14).36 Augustine of Hippo even labeled people that consult sortes "foes of God" (inimici Dei, omnes consultores sortilegorum).37 William Klingshirn has examined the extent to which lot divination encountered ecclesiastical resistance in the West, especially Gaul. The strict prohibitions not only give an indication of early church leaders' anxieties, they also show that lot divination was practiced widely in that region and even conducted by clergy themselves.38 What makes divination so contentious, so dangerous to the leadership? In order to grasp what is at stake, I argue, building on Laura Nasrallah's work in her book An Ecstasy of Folly, that this is an epistemological concern.39 At stake in the discourse on divination is access to knowledge: knowledge about political developments such as the life and especially death of emperors, knowledge about everyday concerns, and knowledge of (or access to) God. The Gospel of the Lots of Mary There is much we do not know about our text. Unlike other ancient texts, the Gospel of the Lots of Mary does not mention an author, not even under a pseudonym. We also do not learn of specific addressees. The place and date of its composition remain unknown. Some of these features our text shares with other Gospels. But unlike other Gospels, which have a long history of scholarship, beginning already in antiquity, no ancient writer referred explicitly to our text, whether approvingly or disapprovingly. Thus, we are left to piece together what we can from the text itself. This book presents the first critical edition and English translation of a new text. It also places this text and the miniature codex within the broader framework of the social history and religious practice in Late Antiquity, with a focus on divination. Precisely because texts such as these were often condemned or considered marginal, the interpretation of this text represents a form of Christianity that is less widely known – one that focuses on non-elites. 36 See also 2Kings 17:17–8. 37 "Ergo inimici Dei omnes amatores mundi, omnes inquisitors nugarum, omnes consultores sortilegorum, mathematicorum, pythonum" (Enarr. in Ps. XCI 10, quoted from Weiland, Oordeel der Kerkvaders, 10 n.1). In Enarr. in Ps. CXL. 18 (ibid. 10 n.2) the word sortilegos is mentioned again. On Augustine's attitude towards divination and divine communication, see Klingshirn, "Divination and the Disciplines of Knowledge". 38 Klingshirn, "Christian Divination". 39 See Nasrallah, Ecstasy of Folly.  Introduction 10 The book consists of two parts. The edition of the Coptic text, my translation and a textual commentary, and images of the manuscript make up Part II. In the first chapter of Part I, I open the codex and begin to read its text. I consider why the book is called a gospel, given that it is so different in content from our expectations of Christian books. I will also examine the appearances of the text's characters: Mary, the archangels Gabriel and Michael, God and Jesus, and, generically, "enemies". Then I discuss the text's striking theology, showing that we have entered a world that is both familiarly Christian and at the same time strange and unknown. This everyday text provides fascinating glimpses into a milieu that is otherwise difficult to see: it is thoroughly Christianized, yet not Christo-centric; larded with biblical allusions, yet Jesus Christ plays a marginal role. Finally, I examine the text's exclusive focus on the client. The second chapter takes a closer look at the codex as artifact. This entails an examination of codicology and palaeography, since both help to establish a date for the codex. I also investigate the possible provenance and context of this book and discuss possible reasons for its miniature format. In the third chapter we encounter the book's users: diviner and client. Here I explore the way the book functioned for each by examining its material format, the layout of the pages, and the instructions provided in various other divinatory texts. Finally, in the fourth chapter I contextualize our codex within the wide-ranging ancient discourse on divination. Those advocating the prohibition of divination had strong voices. Conversely, the other side in this debate has been largely silent (or silenced), yet also resilient. The people who composed our text, or those who practiced divination with this codex, have left no musings about what they thought about and did with lot texts. We can, of course, read the church canons and other prohibitions against the grain to reconstruct the positions they forbid. With this little codex, we have a well-preserved voice in defense of divination. Thus I view this book in its entirety, as text and artifact, as a participant in the larger debate on divination and access to divine foreknowledge in antiquity. As such, this miniature codex, which asserts its own trustworthiness and reliability, preserves an oft-neglected perspective in the controversy about access to God. We hear that voice in multiple resonances through its text: in its title, proudly claiming to be a gospel, its answers full of biblical allusions, the exhortations to trust it, and also through its materiality: in its probable archaeological provenance and connection with church spaces and Christian clergy. Indeed, this little codex has a much larger story to tell.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: Let me start with how this manuscript came to light.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: A curator at Harvard's Sackler Museum reached out to a doctoral student a few days before Christmas, asking her to examine a Coptic book.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: The student, assuming it was a nineteenth-century printed text, asked what kind of book it was.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: The answer came back, a sixth-century manuscript.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: The next day she went to the museum with a notebook, a camera, a tripod, and considerable curiosity.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: When the curator unwrapped a stack of tiny pages bound in brown leather, the first thing that struck her was the size codex was no larger than her palm.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: On the first page she read the title The Gospel of the Lots of Mary, the Mother of the Lord Jesus Christ, that raised immediate questions.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: What kind of gospel is this?

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: What does it contain?

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: Who owned it and used it, and why is it so small?

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: Over the past century manuscript discoveries have dramatically expanded our library of ancient Christian texts.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: We now have the Gospels of Mary and Thomas, and more recently the Gospel of Judas.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: These finds have enriched our understanding of early Christianity considerably.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: But this new gospel turns out to be very different in both content and contribution.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: It is not a narrative about Jesus at all.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: It contains no story, no plot, no sayings of Jesus.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: In fact, Jesus appears only occasionally.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: Instead, the book holds a series of oracular answers meant to be received in a divinatory session.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: These oracles were not designed to be read in sequence.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: From beginning to end each one was meant to be consulted individually, retrieved through a divinatory procedure involving lots.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: The book is laid out so that, when opened, the two facing pages display exactly one oracle at a time.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: People facing difficult decisions or seeking insight into the future would go to a diviner who would perform a ritual to locate an oracle in the codex and then interpret the text for the client.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: This practice, known as sortanish, was both common and controversial in Egypt and across the wider Mediterranean world.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: Now sortalage is a term that may be unfamiliar, so let me define it clearly.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: Sortalage is divination by casting lot to obtain oracular answers.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: The word itself comes from the Latin surs, meaning lot.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: Despite being relatively understudied in modern scholarship on ancient religion, sortalage was not a fringe phenomenon.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: On the contrary, lot divination was widely practiced in antiquity, just as it is in many cultures today.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: Its prevalence is attested even in biblical traditions.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: Not all biblical authors have proved of divination, to be sure, but both the Hebrew scriptures and the New Testament are full of instances where casting lots determines someone's fate.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: The sentiment behind many of these lot decisions is captured in Proverbs 16.33, which says that the lot has cast into the lap, but the decision is the Lord's alone.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: The point is that the divine will determines how the lots fall.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: This is exactly what happens in the story of Jonah.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: In that book sailors call him a terrible storm, and facing shipwreck, cast lots to find out who had brought calamity upon their voyage.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: The lot falls on Jonah, who had rebelled against God's command to preach to Nineveh.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: When his shipmates throw him overboard, the storm subsides.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: The reader expects this outcome, but the point is that the lots reveal divine judgment.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: The New Testament authors similarly interpret the outcome of lot divination as a divine decision.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: Consider the weighty matter of choosing Judas' replacement, the twelfth disciple.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: The remaining eleven apostles turn to sortalage.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: First they pray to the Lord an important aspect of divination that is also prescribed in later books of lot oracles.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: Then they cast lots, and the lot falls on Matthias, who is added to the eleven apostles.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: The text reports this matter of factly as if it were the most natural thing in the world, because the practice of casting lots is treated positively in the stories of Jonah and Matthias.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: The Christian lot books repeatedly refer back to these two episodes, to legitimize their own controversial oracular practices.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: If the Bible itself showed lots revealing God's will, then a Christian book of oracles could claim the same authority.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: There is a technical point worth understanding here about how sortalage works.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: Scholars of divination call it randomization.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: Articipoli ensure that the lots or dice are allowed to move freely and randomly, right up to the moment they give their answer, whether by emerging from a jar or coming to a stop on a table.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: Those who use these methods understand then to guarantee that no human being can predetermine the outcome.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: The randomness leaves room for superhuman agents is to intervene and guide the objects, So the very randomness of the procedure is what makes it a vehicle for divine will.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: In antiquity divinatory practices permeate in every level of society.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: For many people today the word oracle brings to mind the mysterious Pythia at Delphi, delivering war strategies to kings in obscure hexameter verses.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: Or perhaps it calls to mind Alexander the Great, who made an arduous journey through the Egyptian desert to ask the Siwa oracle whether he was indeed the son of God.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: But seeking oracles to obtain divinely inspired answers was not exclusively the province of the elite.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: Enslaved people consulted lot oracles about gaining their freedom, pregnant women asked about giving birth, merchants wanted to know about success in business, travelers inquired about their voyage home, emperors sought insight about the outcomes of battles.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: The evidence for this ubiquity comes from many directions, impressive inscribed monuments erected in public places in Asia Minor, small strips of papyrus folded into tiny sealed packages from an Egyptian martyr shrine, and our new codex itself, epigraphic and manuscript evidence together show that sortilage was everywhere in the ancient Mediterranean world.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: Where could one consult an oracle in antiquity?

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: The possibilities ranged from grand sites like Delphi to a diviner with a book who would visit the inquirer at home.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: Some people travelled great distances to the oracles of Delphi, Dedima or Claro's sites that, as we know from inscriptions, welcomed visitors from all over the region.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: Rich people could send slaves to submit questions on their behalf, but there were also opportunities to consult the divine without travelling to an oracular site at all.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: Book oracles, called sortes, allowed for consultation on the spot.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: The oracle could even come to the petitioner.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: Scholars have described these sortes as instant oracles, or as oracles that preceded the event, ta pre-existent answer waiting for the question to arrive.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: Our codex is exactly this kind of mobile, ready-made tool for divination.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: It is a book that brings the oracle to you, wherever you happen to be, so let me pull together what we have.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: This tiny sixth-century Coptic manuscript, discovered in a museum collection, turns out to be a previously unknown Christian divinatory text.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: It calls itself a gospel.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: But it is not a narrative gospel in any conventional sense, it is a collection of oracular answers, designed to be consulted one at a time through a ritual of casting lots to practice it represents.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: Sortilage was widespread throughout antiquity, attested in the Bible itself, and in the daily lives of people from every social stratum.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: The stories of Jonah and Matthias provided biblical precedents that later Christian lot books used to justify their own existence.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: And the very mechanics of the practice, the randomization of the lots, were understood as the means by which divine will could express itself.

units.lesson: 01 - Discovery and Nature of the Gospel of the Lots of Mary
units.text: This little book, small enough to fit in a palm, is a window into a world where the divine could be consulted on demand, where the sacred was portable, and where the line between acceptable and forbidden religious practice was very much in dispute.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: Let's begin with the family our codex belongs to.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: It's part of a large Mediterranean family of lot books, a clan that includes inscriptions, papyri and parchment manuscripts written in Greek, Latin, Hebrew, Syriac, Provençal and Coptic.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: These texts are called sortes, and they share several defining traits that let scholars study them as a subgenre of oracles.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: These work through the drawing of lots, the casting of dice, or other randomizing practices.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: They address the inquirer directly in the second person singular.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: Their answers come in prose, not in the poetic hexameters, typical of other oracles, and they present a binary worldview with stark contrasts between good and bad outcomes.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: The world they depict is full of adversaries and enemies, with the threat of danger, illness and death shadowing the inquirer.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: But they also promise happiness, a good life, abundant harvest and prosperity.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: Despite these shared features, the sortes family shows considerable diversity, especially in how consultation works.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: Some lot books present clients with pre-formulated questions and matching answers, people wondering am I to become successful, or will the one who is sick survive, or am I to escape from slander, could consult a Greek system called the sortes astramsiki.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: This collection had ninety-two questions and one hundred and three answers.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: The inquiry about success might yield the response, You'll soon succeed for the better.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: A person worried about poison could receive the advice, You've indeed been poisoned.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: Treat yourself.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: The many copies preserved in the papyrological record show that the sortes astramsiki were hugely popular in late antiquity.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: They also had a long after-life in different forms.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: A manuscript from Gaul copied around the year 600, called the sortes sangalensis, is a Latin adaptation of the sortes astramsiki, or a similar lot text.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: Ticket oracles are a related system that yields specific answers.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: Here a client submits two almost identical sealed tickets to a shrine, one with a query phrased positively and the other negatively.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: The priests hand back the ticket, with the correct formulation as the divine answer.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: We have such tickets in Demotic, Coptic and Greek in rare cases, both tickets survive.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: A Greek example from the shrine of St.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: Philoxenus in Oxyrhynchus in the sixth century shows how this worked.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: One ticket asks whether it is God's will that the inquirer take the banking business, and if so, bids him learn this and speak.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: Its twin asks whether it is not God's will that he speak about the bank or the weighing office, and if so, bids him learn this in order not to speak.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: We will probably never know if the inquirer became a banker, but when he received back one of the tickets, we at least knew what to do.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: Our text belongs to the second type of lot system, where a client could pose any question and would receive a general answer.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: The satirist Lucian of Samosata called such responses obscure and ambiguous.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: This vagueness was not the mistake of careless or ignorant composers, but was deliberate.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: Ethnographic research into divinatory practices in Africa has shown that the ambiguity of oracular answers serves a clear purpose.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: It allows openings in the dialogue between the diviner and the client.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: Oracles require interpretation, the general and deliberately ambiguous wording of the sorts, like that in a newspaper horoscope or fortune cookie today, made them adaptable to any situation, but it also increased the hermeneutical vulnerability that Lucian exploits in his satire.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: Some divinatory books spring from sacred texts.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: The Greek sortes Homericae and the Latin sorts Virgiliae consist of abstracts and selected sentences from Homer and Virgil respectively.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: In Jewish and later Christian circles the system was applied to the Bible, giving rise to the sortes bibliae in Greek.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: This category also includes the hermeneae manuscripts, where short divinatory phrases preceded by the Greek word hermania, meaning explanation, are penned in the margins of biblical books, most often in the Gospel of John.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: These exist in Greek and Coptic.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: Another branch of the sortes are the dice, oracles.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: These are Greek texts incised on large monuments and prominently displayed in the marketplaces of cities and towns in southwestern Anatolia.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: Fritz Graf's study of these inscriptions showed how their placement in the public square reveals their broader function in ancient society.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: As these texts gave divinely inspired advice on matters such as commerce, travel, family life and health, when it comes to language, the entire sortes family has only a few Coptic members or more, accurately, few Coptic manuscripts have been published.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: Besides our new text, the longest Coptic sortes text is a seventh or eighth century papyrus codex of unknown provenance, now at the Vatican Library, edited by Arnold van Lanchut in 1956.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: Although both texts share verbal similarities, the Vatican manuscript has short numbered answers that differ substantially from our codex, which gives longer, more general answers.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: The most important other Coptic sortes manuscript for our booklet is its text's closest relative.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: This is an early seventh century manuscript, consisting of two palimpsest fragments from a parchment codex founded the Church of St.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: Colufus in Antinomo, published by Lucia Papini in 1998.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: On the broken bifolium only four answers remain of what was presumably a larger codex.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: Two of those answers are almost verbatim parallel with our codex's text, while the other two share sentences with our text, but in a different order.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: With their focus on solving everyday problems, lot books provide rich material for social historians.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: Palimlia Athanasiade remarked that oracles were the psychiatrists of the ancient world and much more than that.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: When in distress, the individual had recourse to Apollo and usually went away with renewed confidence in the future.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: Throughout antiquity, consultation on private matters remained a normal oracular function.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: Through these texts we enter a world both radically different from ours, and yet strikingly similar, lot texts give us glimpses into everyday anxieties.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: A sense of real physical vulnerability about health, travel, love, and professional success is still very recognizable even if mediated by texts, to appreciate these texts as artifacts of the ancient past.

units.text: We must understand the role and function of sortes and other divinatory texts in antiquity, as tools for religious consultation about large and small concerns.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: In the past some scholars looked down on sortilage.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: Otto Stegmüller missed the point when he disparagingly stated about a papyrus with hermenaeum marginalia, that as regards their content, these oracles are obviously worthless.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: But those who engaged in divination took it seriously, even if others mortalized it, and we moderns may be uneasy with it, while some ancient authors, such as Cicero and Lucian of Samosata, pointed to the potential for corruption and manipulation.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: We should presuppose the religious and thus practical significance of divination in the everyday lives of people.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: In flights of ethnographers, such as David Zitlin, have helped grasp this more fully.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: Zitlin observes that it is possible to do divination as a game, as a procedure without any cognitive or emotional load being carried.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: However, such cases are aberrant, they point to the usual perceived purpose of divination.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: To find answers to questions generally, divination is used as a means of resolving problems.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: Many currently working on the topic recognize full well that these practices were an important means of decision-making in antiquity.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: Thus divination is also intensely related to power and authority, group formation and group identity.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: That divination was ubiquitous, and taken seriously by its ancient practitioners is clear from the ways in which it was contested by secular laws and church canons that prohibit these divinatory practices in no uncertain terms, deeming them inappropriate and dangerous.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: Government officials and emperors issued decrees against divination, for instance in 199 Shii.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: The Egyptian prefect sent out a circular that was to be posted in public, stipulating that all who were found to engage in divination or magic would be put to death.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: Similarly the historian Ammianus Marcellinus reports the forced closing of the bees-ticket oracle in Avidos Phaeum at the orders of Emperor Constantius in the year 359.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: Church leaders also condemned Christian divination, naming it among a series of crimes that Christians should not commit, and forbidding it repeatedly at church councils.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: Although we observed earlier instances, where lot divination was practiced in biblical writings, church leaders could also fall back on biblical prohibitions of such practices.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: One law prescribed that when you come into the land that the Lord your God has given you, you must not learn to imitate the abhorrent practices of those nations.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: No one shall be found among you who makes a son or daughter pass through fire, or who practices divination, or is a soothsayer, or an augur, or one who casts spells, or one who consults ghosts or spirits, or who seeks oracles from the dead, although these nations that you are about to dispossess do give heed to soothsayers and diviners.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: As for you, the Lord your God does not permit you to do so.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: Augustine of Hippo even labeled people who consult sortes foes of God.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: William Clingshurn has examined the extent to which lot divination encountered ecclesiastical resistance in the West, especially Gaul.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: The strict prohibitions not only give an indication of early church leaders' anxieties, they also show that lot divination was practiced widely in that region, and even conducted by clergy themselves.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: What makes divination so contentious, so dangerous to the leadership building on Laura Nasralla's work?

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: The argument is that this is an epistemological concern.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: At stake in the discourse on divination is access to knowledge, knowledge about political developments such as the life and especially death of emperors, knowledge about everyday concerns, and knowledge of or access to God.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: There is much we do not know about our text.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: Unlike other ancient texts, the Gospel of the Locks of Mary does not mention an author, not even under a pseudonym.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: We also do not learn of specific adresies.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: The place and date of its composition remain unknown.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: Some of these features our text shares with other Gospels, but unlike other Gospels which have a long history of scholarship, beginning already in antiquity, no ancient writer referred explicitly to our text, whether approvingly or disapprovingly.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: Thus we are left to piece together what we can from the text itself.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: This book presents the first critical edition and English translation of this new text.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: It also places the text and the miniature codex within the broader framework of the social history and religious practice in late antiquity with a focus on divination, precisely because texts such as these were often condemned or considered marginal.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: The interpretation of this text represents a form of Christianity that is less widely known.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: One that focuses on non-elites, the book consists of two parts.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: The edition of the Coptic text, the translation, a textual commentary, and images of the manuscript make up Part T, Part Y, as four chapters.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: In the first chapter I open the codex and begin to read its text.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: I consider why the book is called a Gospel given, that it is so different in content from our expectations of Christian books.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: I examine the appearances of the text's characters, Mary, the archangels, Gabriel and Michael, God and Jesus, and generically enemies.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: Then I discuss the text's striking theology, showing that we have entered a world that is both familiarly Christian and at the same time strange and unknown.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: This everyday text provides fascinating glimpses into a milieu that is otherwise difficult to see.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: It is thoroughly Christianized, yet not Christo-sylloch, larded with biblical allusions.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: Yet Jesus Christ plays a marginal role.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: Finally, I examine the text's exclusive focus on the client.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: The second chapter takes a closer look at the codex as Beckett.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: This entails an examination of codicology and paleography, since both help to establish a date for the codex.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: I also investigate the possible provenance and context of this book and discuss possible reasons for its miniature formats.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: In the third chapter we encounter the book's users, diviner and client.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: Here I explore the way the book functioned for each by examining its material format, the layout of the pages, and the instructions provided in various other divinatory texts.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: Finally, in the fourth chapter I contextualize our codex within the wide-ranging ancient discourse on divination.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: Those advocating the prohibition of divination had strong voices.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: Conversely, the other side in this debate has been largely silent or silenced, yet also resilient.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: The people who composed our text, or those who practiced divination, with this codex have left no musings about what they thought about and did with lot texts.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: We can, of course, read the church cadence and other prohibitions against the grain to reconstruct the positions they forbid.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: With this little codex we have a well-preserved voice in defense of divination.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: Thus I view this book in its entirety, as text and bequeat, as a participant in the larger debate on divination and access to divine foreknowledge in antiquity.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: As such, this miniature codex, which asserts its own trustworthiness and reliability, preserves an oft-neglected perspective in the controversy about access to God.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: We hear that voice in multiple resonances through its text.

units.lesson: 02 - Sortes Books and Oracles in Context
units.text: In its title, proudly claiming to be a gospel, its answer is full of biblical allusions, the exhortations to trust it, and also, through its materiality, in its probable archaeological provenance and connection with church spaces and Christian clergy, indeed this little codex has a much larger story to tell.
